# Italian {#sec-italian}

*Padre nostro.* Italian sits closer to the Latin of the
[Latin chapter](latin.qmd) than any other language here, and the prayer shows
it — *rimetti a noi i nostri debiti* is *dimitte nobis debita nostra* with the
endings worn down. It is also the language in which the sixth petition was
most publicly argued over, and the only one in this book whose official text
changed in living memory.

## Catholic liturgical text

The translation in the third edition of the Italian Missal, in use since
29 November 2020.

::: {.prayer lang="it" speech="it-IT" #it-cei}
| Padre nostro, che sei nei cieli,
| sia santificato il tuo nome,
| venga il tuo regno,
| sia fatta la tua volontà, come in cielo così in terra.
| Dacci oggi il nostro pane quotidiano,
| e rimetti a noi i nostri debiti
| come anche noi li rimettiamo ai nostri debitori,
| e non abbandonarci alla tentazione,
| ma liberaci dal male.
:::

## The sentence that changed

For most of the twentieth century Italians prayed *e non ci indurre in
tentazione* — "and lead us not into temptation", the sixth petition as the
Latin has it and as English still has it. The 2008 CEI translation of Matthew
replaced it, and in 2020 the new Missal carried the change into the Mass
itself:

> *e non ci indurre in tentazione* → *e non abbandonarci alla tentazione*

"Do not abandon us to temptation". The objection it answers is old and blunt:
the older wording seems to make God the one doing the leading. The same
edition added a single word to the fifth petition, *come **anche** noi li
rimettiamo* — "as we **too** forgive" — and the Latin *editio typica* was
never touched at all.

Italy was not alone. France made the same move in 2017, and the reasoning is
the one behind the Lithuanian Catholic *neleisk mūsų gundyti*
([Lithuanian](lithuanian.qmd)) and the demotic Greek *να μην επιτρέψεις να
υποκύψουμε* ([Modern Greek](modern-greek.qmd)). Three languages, three
different centuries, one uncomfortable verb.

## Waldensian text

The version used by the Chiesa evangelica valdese, Italy's oldest Protestant
church.

::: {.prayer lang="it" speech="it-IT" #it-valdese .variant}
| Padre nostro, che sei nei cieli,
| sia santificato il tuo nome,
| venga il tuo regno,
| sia fatta la tua volontà, come in cielo anche in terra.
| Dacci oggi il nostro pane necessario,
| e rimetti a noi i nostri debiti,
| come anche noi li rimettiamo ai nostri debitori
| e non esporci alla tentazione,
| ma liberaci dal Male.
| Tuo è il Regno, la potenza e la gloria nei secoli dei secoli.
| Amen.
:::

Four differences from the Catholic text, and each one is a decision. *Anche in
terra* rather than *così in terra*. *Pane necessario* — "necessary bread" —
where the Catholic text keeps *quotidiano*, a rendering of ἐπιούσιον that
sides with the [Modern Greek](modern-greek.qmd) reading over Jerome's. *Non
esporci alla tentazione*, "do not expose us to temptation", a third answer to
the same problem. And *dal Male* capitalised: the Evil One, not evil, the
distinction the *Nova Vulgata* makes in [Latin](latin.qmd).

The doxology is there too, as it is in Protestant usage generally and absent
from the Catholic text, which reaches it only after the embolism.

## Amen

Italian Catholics do not say *Amen* at the end of the Lord's Prayer at Mass —
the prayer runs straight into the embolism, and the *Amen* belongs to the
doxology that follows it.
